paragraphs: General Ideas Than Their Forefathers, the English.

God does not regard the human race as a whole. He surveys all the beings that make up mankind at a single glance and one by one. In each person he sees both the resemblances that tie him to his fellows and the differences that set him apart from them. God therefore has no need of general ideas. That is, he never feels any need to gather a large number of similar things under one form to make thinking easier. Man is in a different position. If the human mind tried to examine and judge every individual case that came before it, the sheer mass of detail would soon lead it astray and confuse its judgment. In this difficulty man turns to an expedient that is imperfect but necessary, and that both helps him and exposes his weakness. He considers a certain number of things superficially and notices that they resemble one another. Then he gives them a common name, sets them apart, and moves on.

General ideas are no proof of the strength of the human intellect. They show rather its inadequacy. For nature contains no two beings exactly alike, no two things precisely identical, and no rule that applies indiscriminately and equally to several objects at once. The chief merit of general ideas is that they let the human mind pass a quick judgment on a great many objects at once. On the other hand, the notions they convey are always incomplete, and they always make the mind lose as much in accuracy as it gains in breadth. As societies advance in civilization, they learn new facts, and each day they pick up, almost without noticing, some particular truths. The more truths of this kind a man grasps, the more general ideas he is naturally led to form. A multitude of particular facts cannot be seen separately without eventually revealing the common tie that connects them. Several individuals lead to the perception of the species, and several species to that of the genus. The habit and the taste for general ideas will therefore always be strongest among a people of long-established culture and extensive knowledge.
But there are other reasons that push men to generalize their ideas, or hold them back from doing so.

The Americans are much more given to the use of general ideas than the English, and have a much greater taste for them. At first sight this seems very strange, when we remember that the two nations have the same origin, that they lived for centuries under the same laws, and that they still constantly exchange their opinions and their manners. The contrast becomes much more striking if we look at our own part of the world and compare the two most educated nations that live in it. The English mind seems able to tear itself away from the observation of particular facts, and rise from them to their causes, only reluctantly and painfully. It seems to generalize only in spite of itself. Among the French, on the contrary, the taste for general ideas seems to have grown into so ardent a passion that it must be satisfied on every occasion. Every morning when I wake I am told that some general and eternal law has just been discovered, one I had never heard mentioned before. There is not a mediocre scribbler who does not try his hand at discovering truths that apply to a great kingdom, and who is not very displeased with himself if he fails to squeeze the human race into the space of an article. It surprises me that two very educated nations should differ so much. If I turn my attention back to England and look at the events there over the last half-century, I think I can affirm that the taste for general ideas grows in that country in proportion as its ancient constitution weakens.

The state of civilization is therefore not enough by itself to explain what prompts the human mind to love general ideas or turns it away from them. When the conditions of men are very unequal, and inequality is the permanent state of society, individuals gradually become so unlike one another that each class takes on the appearance of a separate race. Only one of these classes is in view at any moment. People lose sight of the general tie that binds them all within the vast bosom of mankind, and their observation always settles not on man but on certain men. Those who live in this aristocratic state of society therefore never form very general ideas about themselves. That is enough to give them a habitual distrust of such ideas and an instinctive aversion to them. The man who lives in a democratic country, on the contrary, sees men all around him who differ very little from one another. He cannot turn his mind to any one part of mankind without his thought expanding until it takes in the whole. All the truths that apply to himself seem to him equally and similarly applicable to each of his fellow citizens and fellow men. He acquires the habit of generalizing his ideas in the study that occupies him most and interests him more than any other, and he carries the same habit into all his pursuits. This is how the craving to discover general laws in everything, to bring a great number of objects under a single formula, and to explain a mass of facts by one cause becomes an ardent and sometimes undiscerning passion of the human mind.

Nothing shows the truth of this proposition more clearly than the opinions the ancients held about their slaves. The deepest and most capacious minds of Rome and Greece never managed to reach the idea, at once so general and so simple, that all men are alike and that each has the same birthright to freedom. They tried to prove that slavery was part of the order of nature and would always exist. More than that, everything shows that those among the ancients who had passed from slavery to freedom, many of whom have left us excellent writings, themselves viewed servitude in no other light.

All the great writers of antiquity belonged to the aristocracy of masters, or at least saw that aristocracy established and uncontested before their eyes. Their minds, after expanding in several directions, were blocked from further progress in this one. The coming of Jesus Christ to earth was needed to teach that all members of the human race are by nature equal and alike.

In ages of equality all men are independent of one another, isolated and weak. The movements of the multitude are not permanently guided by the will of any individuals. At such times humanity seems always to advance by itself. To explain what is happening in the world, a man is therefore driven to look for some great causes that act in the same way on all his fellow creatures and so push them all, against their will, along the same track. This in turn naturally leads the human mind to form general ideas, and gives it a taste for them.

I have already shown how the equality of conditions leads every man to investigate truths for himself. It is easy to see that a method of this kind must gradually and imperceptibly produce a tendency toward general ideas in the human mind. When I reject the traditions of rank, profession, and birth, and when I escape the authority of example to find the path I should follow by the sole effort of my own reason, I am inclined to draw the grounds of my opinions from human nature itself. This leads me necessarily, and almost without noticing, to adopt a great number of very general notions.

All that I have said here explains why the English show much less readiness and taste for generalizing ideas than their American offspring, and still less than their French neighbors. It also explains why the English of today show more of these qualities than their forefathers did. The English have long been a very educated and very aristocratic nation. Their education urged them constantly to generalize, and their aristocratic habits confined them to particulars. From this came the philosophy, at once bold and timid, broad and narrow, that has prevailed in England until now, and that still obstructs and stagnates so many minds in that country.

Apart from the causes I have pointed out above, others can be discerned that are less obvious but no less effective, and that give almost every democratic people a taste, and often a passion, for general ideas. A careful distinction must be made between ideas of this kind. Some are the result of slow, detailed, and conscientious labor of the mind, and these widen the sphere of human knowledge. Others spring up at once from the first quick exercise of the wits, and produce only very superficial and very uncertain notions. People who live in ages of equality have a great deal of curiosity and very little leisure. Their lives are so practical, so confused, so excited, and so active that little time is left to them for thought. Such people are drawn to general ideas because these spare them the trouble of studying particulars. General ideas contain, so to speak, a great deal in a small space, and give a large return in a short time. So if a brief and inattentive investigation leads them to think they have detected a common relation among certain objects, they push the inquiry no further. Without examining in detail how far these different objects differ or agree, they quickly arrange them under one formula so that they can move on to another subject.

One of the distinguishing characteristics of a democratic period is the taste all men have at such times for easy success and immediate enjoyment. This is true of the pursuits of the intellect as of all others. Most of those who live in a time of equality are full of an ambition that is at once aspiring and slack. They would like to succeed brilliantly and at once, but they would be excused from great efforts to achieve success. These conflicting tendencies lead straight to the pursuit of general ideas. With the help of such ideas they flatter themselves that they can cut a very important figure at small expense and attract the public’s attention with very little trouble. And I do not know whether they are wrong to think so. For their readers are as unwilling to investigate anything to the bottom as they are themselves, and what people generally look for in the products of the mind is easy pleasure and information without labor.

Aristocratic nations do not make enough use of general ideas, and they often treat them with thoughtless disdain. It is true, on the other hand, that a democratic people is always ready to carry ideas of this kind to excess and to embrace them with injudicious warmth.
